extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP counsel and in-house counsel practising or considering litigation before the Unified Patent Court (Europe)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and procedural guidance for bringing, defending and managing patent actions before the Unified Patent Court (UPC), including jurisdiction, court structure, remedies, procedure and strategic considerations across participating EU states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation and ratification of the UPCA
rubrics_metrics.description: Any full member state of the European Union has the option to participate; to participate in the Court procedure signatories must formally ratify the Unified Patent Court Agreement (UPCA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of 30 June 2025, 18 EU member states have formally ratified the UPCA (list provided). Spain, Poland and Croatia chose not to sign the UPCA in 2013; other signatories (Cyprus, Czechia, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Slovakia) are yet to ratify. The UK withdrew following Brexit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents within UPC jurisdiction and opt-out rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Default position: all European patents designated in participating member states are within the jurisdiction of the UPC, but owners of extant patents may opt out of the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There was a sunrise period prior to commencement for patentees to notify the court of opt-outs. During a seven-year transitional period from commencement, patent owners can still opt out patents. Once opted out, a patent is outside the UPC for its full life unless the owner opts back in; once opted back in, it cannot be opted out again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary Patent option for new applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: New applicants may seek a UP designation, which gives rise to a single Unitary Patent across the full scope of participating member states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National designations remain available for non-participating or non-EU countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the UPC — tiers and referrals
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC has two tiers: first instance Local Divisions, Regional Division and a Central Division; above that sits a single Court of Appeal. Specific questions of EU law can be referred to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court of Appeal's role is to create consistency across divisions and develop clear doctrines on key patent law issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local and Regional Divisions — entitlement and regional arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participating country is entitled to host a Local Division; groups of countries may establish a Regional Division covering several states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germany was allowed four Local Divisions due to case volume. Only one Regional Division (Baltic Division) currently exists covering Sweden, Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania. Countries yet to establish Local Divisions must have cases commenced in appropriate Central Division seats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central Division seats and technology allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Central Division has its seat in Paris, with sections in Milan and Munich; it primarily deals with revocation actions and declarations of non-infringement and allocates cases based on patent technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocation by International Patent Classification: Milan – Class A (Human Necessities, including pharmaceuticals); Munich – Classes C and F (Chemistry, metallurgy and mechanical engineering); Paris – Classes B, D, E, G and M (Physics and electronics plus SPC matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of Appeal role — harmonisation of jurisprudence
rubrics_metrics.description: The single Court of Appeal (based in Luxembourg) is intended to bring together decisions and create a consistent jurisprudence across divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key doctrinal areas where the Court of Appeal is crucial include the doctrine of equivalents, file wrapper estoppel and approaches to claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial composition of panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel composition differs by division: Local/Regional Divisions typically hear cases with three legally qualified judges and one technically qualified judge; Central Division panels comprise two legally qualified judges and one technically qualified judge; the Court of Appeal comprises three legally and two technically qualified judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediators and arbitrators are also part of the system and are subject to training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training of judges, mediators and arbitrators
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges, mediators and arbitrators are regularly trained to support consistent decision-making across the UPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The training centre in Budapest is pending ratification by Hungary; training currently takes place in other locations selected by the Court on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case Management System (CMS) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: All divisions and levels can be commenced and managed using the UPC’s Case Management System (CMS), an online resource governing commencement and management of UPC cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users should use the CMS for case filings and management; further information is available on the UPC’s website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of Procedure of the UPC
rubrics_metrics.description: All first instance Divisions and the Court of Appeal are operated in accordance with the Rules of Procedure of the Unified Patent Court, a comprehensive set of procedural rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a question of EU law is referred to the CJEU then the CJEU’s procedural rules apply. The UPC Rules are an amalgam of rules from many participating countries and include influences from UK procedure as used during preparatory stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict timescale objective for case completion (~12 months)
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC Rules stipulate a strict timescale with the objective that all cases should be completed approximately 12 months after commencement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The objective supports delivery of effective and high-quality justice in a timely fashion; parties and advisers should plan case conduct accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content of initial pleadings and evidence rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules govern the necessary content of initial pleadings and contain detailed provisions regarding evidence gathering, conduct of experiments, possible cross-examination of witnesses, and very limited orders for disclosure of documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must ensure initial pleadings meet the stipulated content requirements and be prepared for tightly regulated evidentiary procedures (limited disclosure, possible experiments and witness cross-examination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for significant cost recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC contains provisions for significant cost recovery by the successful parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such provisions are notable because significant cost recovery is generally not common in European patent litigation; cost risk should inform litigation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement actions should be brought in the Local or Regional Division for the country where the defendant is domiciled; if that country has no Local/Regional Division, the action can be brought in the appropriate seat of the Central Division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, infringement actions can be brought before the Local/Regional Division where the actual or threatened infringement has occurred or may occur. The Rules align with the Recast Brussels Regulation and the Lugano Convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for revocation and declarations of non-infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions for revocation or declarations of non-infringement are to be brought in the appropriate seat of the Central Division, with seat determined by technology type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Central Division technology allocation (Milan, Munich, Paris) to determine the correct seat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterclaim for revocation — presumptive stay in Local Division with transfer discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a counterclaim to an infringement action contains a request for revocation, the presumption is that the case will remain in the Local Division where the infringement action was commenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court has discretion to transfer the case to a Central Division where appropriate; to date transfers have been exercised in a limited number of cases, often where a parallel revocation action was pending in a Central Division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions regarding Standard Essential Patents (SEPs) and FRAND counterclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions regarding SEPs can be brought in the UPC; the UPC has reserved the right to set rates for Fair, Reasonable and Non-Discriminatory (FRAND) licence terms by way of a counterclaim to an infringement action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties litigating SEPs should consider FRAND counterclaims and the UPC’s competence to determine FRAND rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive provisions for preliminary relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC Rules include comprehensive provisions for the grant of preliminary relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties seeking early injunctive or provisional measures should evaluate available UPC preliminary relief procedures as part of enforcement strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement — cross-border injunctions and damages
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court finds the patent valid and infringed, it may grant an injunction covering all participating countries if the patent was designated in each of those countries; for Unitary Patents, a full injunction will be automatic. Damages may be recovered for sales in all participating countries where the patent was designated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful enforcement can cover an area of over 300 million consumers and a combined GDP of almost EUR14 trillion; this cross-border effect is a key strategic consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-arm jurisdiction following CJEU (BSH v Electrolux)
rubrics_metrics.description: CJEU case law indicates the jurisdiction of the UPC may extend beyond the boundaries of participating countries: courts of the country where the defendant is domiciled have general jurisdiction over infringement in any country where the patent is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This long-arm jurisdiction can include EU states not participating in the UPC and third countries like the UK and Turkey (where a European patent can be designated). Local Divisions of the UPC have applied this principle several times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centres for Arbitration and Mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two Centres for Arbitration and Mediation of patent disputes (Lisbon and Ljubljana) as part of the UPC system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may consider arbitration or mediation at these centres as alternative dispute resolution pathways to court litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical, division-by-division strategic and tactical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide provides practical information regarding the operation of the various divisions, along with strategic and tactical guidance from experienced firms across Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should consult the division-specific sections for local practice nuances and contributor insights to inform litigation strategy and tactics.
